summary: Fire behaves differently in space, but the research needed to understand it can be difficult to navigate. We built FLARE, a web platform that brings NASA combustion studies, measurements, and source records into one place. Users can ask FLARE AI research questions, explore measured flame-spread data, compare investigations, and match studies to mission conditions such as oxygen, pressure, gravity, and airflow. Each investigation connects users to its original sources so they can look beyond a summary and examine the evidence. A separate satellite viewer lets users explore NASA Earth-observation imagery and thermal detections. Our goal is to make space fire-safety research easier to understand and use, while showing where the available evidence leaves questions unanswered. By helping people move from a question to relevant research, FLARE supports learning and further investigation into safer spacecraft and habitats.
details: We built FLARE to help people work through a practical question: what can existing combustion research tell us about fire safety in a future spacecraft or habitat? NASA has valuable experimental findings, but understanding them often means moving between investigation records, technical reports, and individual measurements. FLARE brings these resources into a connected research workspace. The Investigation Explorer contains 21 curated investigation entries, including studies from BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX, and ACME. Users can browse research by hardware, fuel type, or safety goal, then open a record to examine its purpose, test conditions, findings, and original sources. Our Microgravity Combustion Visualizer makes experimental results easier to explore. It plots 39 BASS-II flame-spread observations from a NASA technical report and lets users inspect the conditions behind individual measurements. The comparison tool places investigations side by side so users can see shared conditions and differences that affect how their results should be interpreted. The Mission Evidence Matcher connects research to a selected environment. Users can adjust oxygen concentration, pressure, gravity, material, and airflow, then review relevant investigations and evidence gaps. Its ranking helps identify useful studies; it does not predict fire probability or certify mission safety. FLARE AI gives users another way into the research. They can ask questions about combustion studies, mission conditions, measurements, or research gaps, then use the investigation records and citations to examine the evidence more closely. A separate Satellite Viewer explores NASA’s Earth-observation data through an interactive globe, thermal detections, and imagery layers. This provides another way to engage with NASA data while keeping Earth observations distinct from spacecraft combustion experiments. We developed the website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for the globe and Leaflet for mapping, and deployed it on Vercel. Our scientific sources include NASA’s Physical Science Informatics repository, technical reports, and published research. The main idea behind FLARE is to connect the steps of research: ask a question, find relevant studies, inspect measurements, compare conditions, and return to the original source. We hope this makes combustion research more approachable for students, educators, and people exploring future mission concepts. FLARE includes an AI research assistant. AI tools also helped prepare this submission and the scripts used to produce our demonstration. The demo uses synthetic narration and original music created with AI assistance. Scientific measurements and satellite data are credited to their cited sources.
